passage: The Windmere zoo announced the birth of a red panda cub on Tuesday, the first born there in its 46 year history. The cub, a female, weighed 118 grams at her first weighing and has been named Sorrel after a public vote that drew more than 5,000 entries. The runner-up name, Juniper, received 1,850 votes to Sorrel's 2,300, with the remainder spread across eight other choices. Keepers say the mother, four year old Mei, is nursing well and that the cub opened her eyes on day eighteen, within the normal range. The father, Bramble, arrived from another collection two years ago as part of a managed breeding program. Visitors will not see the cub for some months, as red panda mothers keep their young in nest boxes until early winter. The zoo will instead stream a den camera on its website during morning hours. Head keeper Fiona Adjei said the birth follows two seasons of failed pairings and credited a redesign of the enclosure, completed in March at a cost of 60,000 dollars, with reducing stress on the animals.
question: What name was given to the red panda cub?

passage: The speed limit on the Orchard Valley road will drop from 55 to 40 miles per hour along the three mile stretch between the creamery and the Bellows Corner junction, the county traffic board decided on Monday by a vote of five to one. The change follows a review that counted 31 crashes on the stretch over five years, eleven of them at the entrance to the farm supply store, where turning trucks cross fast traffic. New signs go up within six weeks, and for the first month drivers will receive warnings rather than tickets. The board rejected a competing proposal to lower the limit only in daylight hours, which the sheriff's office had called unenforceable. A parents group that gathered 640 signatures had asked for a 35 mile per hour limit and flashing beacons at the school bus stops; the board ordered a separate study of the beacons, due in the autumn. Board chair Anders Lovel said the county would repaint the centerline and add rumble strips at the two sharpest bends, work budgeted at 85,000 dollars.
question: What will the new speed limit on the Orchard Valley road be?

passage: A district judge on Friday overturned the permit for the proposed Blackrock quarry, ruling that the county board had failed to consider the operation's effect on the aquifer that feeds wells in the hamlet of Dunmore. Judge Celia Ravenscroft wrote that the board relied on a groundwater study covering only the quarry parcel itself, ignoring test data from 14 nearby wells submitted by residents during the comment period. The permit holder, Stonewell Aggregates, had planned to begin blasting this autumn and said it will appeal. The company may also reapply with a broader study, a process the county estimates would take at least ten months. Residents who brought the case had raised 38,000 dollars for legal costs through suppers and an auction. Their lawyer, Tomas Ilic, called the ruling careful and narrow, noting that the judge rejected two other claims, one about truck noise and one about property values. The quarry as proposed would have produced 300,000 tons of crushed stone a year and employed about 25 people.
question: Which judge overturned the quarry permit?

passage: The Gorse Hill transit authority will renumber and reroute its entire bus network on the first Sunday of October, the biggest overhaul since the system began in 1979. The current nine routes become seven, but buses on the two busiest corridors will run every 12 minutes at peak instead of every 20. The much criticized route 6, which loops through the industrial park in one direction only, disappears entirely; its riders get a new two way service numbered 24 that continues to the regional hospital. Planners say 84 percent of current riders will keep a stop within a quarter mile of the one they use now. The authority will station guides at the central exchange for the first two weeks and mail a folded map to every household, a printing job of 61,000 copies. Fares do not change. The redesign was drawn up after 2,400 survey responses and eleven public meetings, and the authority's manager, Hana Okafor-Reyes, conceded that the eastern orchards lose their Sunday service, the one cut she said the budget forced.
question: What number will the new two way service to the regional hospital carry?

passage: Workers digging foundations for an apartment block on Tanner's Row uncovered a brick lined well containing more than 200 leather shoe soles, offcuts, and wooden lasts, the debris of a cobbler's workshop that stood on the site in the 1780s. Construction paused for twelve days while a small team from the regional heritage unit recorded the find, which also included three clay pipes, a bone comb, and a copper token stamped with a rooster. Unit archaeologist Priya Vasquez said waterlogged wells preserve leather that would rot anywhere else, and called the collection the best picture yet of the town's early shoe trade, which court records suggest supported nine workshops by 1795. The developer, Millbrook Homes, agreed to fund conservation of the leather at an estimated cost of 15,000 dollars and to display a selection in the building's lobby. The well itself, judged unstable, was filled after recording. Building work resumed on Thursday, and the block of 48 flats is still expected to open on schedule next summer. The token will go to the county museum.
question: What image was stamped on the copper token found in the well?

passage: The eleventh annual Saltmarsh cheese festival drew a record 18,500 visitors over two days, straining the shuttle buses and clearing several stalls of stock by Saturday afternoon. Organizers had planned for 15,000 based on last year's gate of 13,200 and were caught short on parking, pressing a mown hayfield into service by noon. Forty-one producers attended, up from 33 last year, and the top prize went to a washed rind cheese called Bell Harbor made by the Twin Alder dairy, a first win for the farm after three years of runner-up finishes. The judges, a panel of five, scored 118 entries across nine classes. The people's choice award, decided by tokens dropped in jars, went instead to a smoked goat cheese from the Hartsell sisters, who sold out of it entirely by Sunday. Festival director Miriam Solano said gate receipts of about 92,000 dollars will fund next year's edition and a new refrigerated storage barn for the producers' cooperative. Two food safety complaints were investigated and both dismissed. Next year's festival moves one week later to avoid the regatta.
question: Which cheese won the top prize at the festival?

passage: Restoration of the Point Severin lighthouse is complete, and the tower will open for guided climbs on weekends beginning next month, the coastal trust said on Wednesday. The three year project cost 1.4 million dollars, about a third more than the first estimate, after masons found the upper gallery's ironwork more corroded than surveys had suggested. Crews repointed 30,000 bricks, recast eight of the gallery's sixteen iron brackets, and rebuilt the lantern room's copper roof using photographs from 1936 as a guide. The original fourth order lens, removed to a museum in 1971, will not return; the trust judged the climb stairs too narrow to insure its transport. A replica lens of acrylic was installed instead, lit by a low power lamp that mariners will not mistake for an active aid. Climbs will be limited to eight visitors at a time on the 141 step stair. Trust director Marta Jensen said volunteer training begins in two weeks and that 60 people have already applied for 24 guide positions. The keeper's cottage tearoom opens the same weekend.
question: How many steps does the lighthouse stair have?

passage: The Ashford school district will cook lunches in its own kitchens again starting in January, ending a nine year contract with an outside caterer and reviving a scratch cooking program that once employed 22 kitchen staff. The board voted six to one for the change after a parent audit found that 38 percent of catered meals were arriving below the required serving temperature and that participation in the lunch program had slid from 71 percent of students to 44 percent since the contract began. The district will spend 310,000 dollars to reequip kitchens at its four schools, drawing on a state grant that covers up to half of such costs. A pilot at Maple Row elementary last spring, run by two rehired cooks, lifted participation at that school back to 66 percent in eight weeks. Menus will rotate on a four week cycle and feature one meatless day, and the district has signed purchase agreements with three farms within the county. The catering firm, Verdant Table, said it disputed the audit's methods but would not bid again. Lunch prices will not change this year.
question: What percentage of catered meals did the parent audit find arriving below the required serving temperature?

passage: A proposal to build eleven wind turbines on the Corbett Ridge drew a crowd of about 300 to the district hall on Tuesday, the largest turnout in memory for a planning hearing. The developer, Aria Renewables, told the panel the project would generate enough power for 26,000 homes and pay the district 480,000 dollars a year in fees, with an additional community fund of 100,000 dollars a year controlled by a local board. Opponents focused on the two turbines closest to the hamlet of Corbett Hollow, which would stand 1,900 feet from the nearest house; the district's own guideline, adopted in 2016, is 2,500 feet. The company said it could relocate one of the two but that moving both would put a turbine on unstable ground above the old mine workings. Supporters, including the volunteer fire company, pointed to the fees, which exceed the district's entire current road budget. The panel closed the hearing after four hours without a vote and set a decision for its December session. Written comments will be accepted for 30 more days.
question: How far from the nearest house would the two closest turbines stand?

passage: A terrier that vanished from a campsite in the Verlain gorge eight days ago was found alive on Monday, forty miles away and on the far side of the river, by a postal carrier who recognized her from a flyer. The dog, a six year old named Pickle, disappeared during a thunderstorm on the last night of her family's holiday. Her owners, the Braithwaites, searched for three days, left a worn shirt and a food station at the campsite, and drove home only after the campground closed for the season. The carrier, Denny Ashworth, spotted the dog sheltering under a fruit stand outside the village of Molsheim and coaxed her into his van with half a sandwich. A scan at the Molsheim clinic matched her microchip within minutes. Pickle had lost two pounds but was otherwise sound, apart from a torn ear the vet judged to be several days old. How she crossed the river is unknown; the nearest bridge is nine miles upstream from the campsite. The Braithwaites made the four hour drive that evening. Ashworth declined the family's posted reward of 500 dollars, asking them to give it to the clinic instead.
question: Who found the missing terrier?
